hypotheses.title: cancel() lacks maker authorization check
hypotheses.description: The `cancel(uint128 orderId)` function retrieves the order and calls `_cancelOrder` without verifying that `msg.sender == order.maker`. Any external caller can cancel any open order, and the refund of locked base tokens is credited to the original maker's balance (not the caller), but the order is removed from the book, destroying the maker's liquidity and any pending fill opportunity.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker observes an open order via `getOrders`/`getOrder`. 2. Attacker calls `cancel(orderId)` directly. 3. `_cancelOrder` unlinks the order and refunds `order.remaining` to `order.maker`. 4. Maker's order is gone; attacker can repeat for every order in the book to grief all market makers.
hypotheses.impact: All open orders can be forcibly removed by any untrusted actor, denying liquidity, breaking MPP settlement routing, and enabling targeted griefing of specific makers (e.g., right before a large fill).
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `if (msg.sender != order.maker) revert Unauthorized();` at the top of `cancel()` (or inside `_cancelOrder`).

hypotheses.title: emergencyWithdraw() bypasses balance check and underflows
hypotheses.description: `emergencyWithdraw` calls `_processWithdrawal`, which performs `balances[user][token] -= amount` and `totalDeposits[token] -= amount` inside an `unchecked` block with no prior balance validation. Any caller can withdraw more than they deposited, causing silent uint128 underflow of their balance and of `totalDeposits`, and draining the contract's token reserves.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker deposits a small amount (or none) of token T. 2. Attacker calls `emergencyWithdraw(T, amount)` with `amount` up to `type(uint128).max`. 3. `_processWithdrawal` underflows `balances[attacker][T]` and `totalDeposits[T]` unchecked, then `safeTransfer`s `amount` of T to the attacker. 4. Attacker repeats for every token held by the contract.
hypotheses.impact: Complete drain of all deposited tokens in the DEX; corrupted `totalDeposits` accounting; other users' funds are unrecoverable.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove `emergencyWithdraw` or gate it behind an owner/role check and add `if (balances[msg.sender][token] < amount) revert InsufficientBalance();` before the unchecked subtraction.

hypotheses.title: fillOrder() allows maker to self-fill and inflate balances
hypotheses.description: `fillOrder` does not prevent `msg.sender == order.maker`. A maker can fill their own order, which debits their quote balance and credits their base balance while also crediting their own quote balance as the maker — netting a free increase in base tokens (the quote debit and maker credit cancel, but the base credit remains). Combined with the fact that the maker's locked base was already deducted at `placeOrder`, this lets the maker mint base tokens out of thin air.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker deposits 1 unit of quote token Q. 2. Attacker places an order selling base token B at price P with amount A (B is deducted from attacker's balance). 3. Attacker calls `fillOrder(orderId, A)` as themselves. 4. Attacker's Q balance is debited `A*P/1e18` and credited the same amount (maker credit), while attacker's B balance is credited `A`. 5. Attacker now holds A more B than before, and can withdraw it.
hypotheses.impact: Unlimited minting of any base token held by the DEX; drains other users' deposits; total insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `if (msg.sender == order.maker) revert Unauthorized();` in `fillOrder`.

hypotheses.title: cancel() allows anyone to cancel any order and steal refund
hypotheses.description: `cancel()` calls `_cancelOrder` without verifying that `msg.sender == order.maker`. Any external actor can cancel any open order, and the refund of `order.remaining` base tokens is credited to `balances[maker][baseToken]` — but the maker's balance is credited, not the caller's. However, the attacker can then immediately fill or withdraw... actually the refund goes to the maker, so the attacker cannot directly steal. But the attacker can grief: cancel any maker's order at will, removing liquidity and forcing the maker's funds back to available balance. This is a griefing/DoS vector against market makers.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker observes an open order ID (public via events/getOrders). 2. Attacker calls `cancel(orderId)`. 3. Order is removed from the linked list and maker's locked tokens are refunded to maker's available balance. 4. Maker's order disappears from the book without consent.
hypotheses.impact: Any untrusted actor can unilaterally cancel every open order in the book, destroying liquidity and disrupting MPP settlement. Makers cannot keep orders live.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `if (msg.sender != order.maker) revert Unauthorized();` in `cancel()` before calling `_cancelOrder`.

hypotheses.title: emergencyWithdraw lacks balance check, allows draining other users' funds
hypotheses.description: `emergencyWithdraw` calls `_processWithdrawal` which performs `balances[user][token] -= amount` inside an `unchecked` block with no prior balance check. If a user's balance is smaller than `amount`, the subtraction underflows silently, wrapping to a huge uint128 value. The contract then transfers `amount` real tokens out, so the user can withdraw more than they deposited, draining tokens that belong to other depositors.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits a tiny amount (e.g. 1 unit) of token T. 2) Attacker calls `emergencyWithdraw(T, X)` where X is any amount up to the contract's total token balance. 3) The unchecked subtraction wraps the attacker's balance to a huge number instead of reverting. 4) `safeTransfer` sends X tokens to the attacker, draining other users' deposits.
hypotheses.impact: Complete loss of all deposited tokens in the contract; protocol becomes insolvent; other users cannot withdraw their funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the `unchecked` block in `_processWithdrawal` and add an explicit `if (balances[user][token] < amount) revert InsufficientBalance();` check before subtracting.

hypotheses.title: cancel() has no maker authorization, anyone can cancel any order
hypotheses.description: `cancel` calls `_cancelOrder` without checking `msg.sender == order.maker`. Any external actor can cancel any open order, refunding the locked base tokens to the maker and removing the order from the book. This lets an attacker grief market makers and manipulate the orderbook at will.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a large maker order in the book. 2) Attacker calls `cancel(orderId)` on that order. 3) The order is removed and the maker's tokens are refunded, disrupting liquidity. 4) Attacker repeats to clear the book or front-run fills.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service for market makers; orderbook can be wiped by any attacker; MPP settlement liquidity disappears; griefing with no cost.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `if (msg.sender != order.maker) revert Unauthorized();` at the start of `cancel`.

hypotheses.title: fillOrder has no minimum-out / slippage parameter for taker
hypotheses.description: `fillOrder(orderId, amount)` computes `quoteAmount` purely from the stored `order.price` and debits the taker with no `minQuoteOut`/`maxQuoteIn` parameter. If the maker's price is stale or manipulated (see above), the taker has no on-chain way to bound the cost. There is also no check that the price is still valid at fill time.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker posts an order at a favorable-to-attacker price. 2) Victim's integration calls `fillOrder` with only `amount`. 3) Victim pays whatever `quoteAmount` the maker set, with no revert path.
hypotheses.impact: Takers can be forced to pay arbitrarily bad prices; direct loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `minQuoteOut` (or `maxQuoteIn`) parameter to `fillOrder` and revert if the computed `quoteAmount` violates it.

hypotheses.title: emergencyWithdraw() decrements before transfer but lacks balance check
hypotheses.description: `_processWithdrawal()` uses `unchecked { balances[user][token] -= amount; totalDeposits[token] -= amount; }` with no prior balance check. Any user can call `emergencyWithdraw()` with an amount exceeding their balance, causing `balances[user][token]` to underflow to a huge value and `totalDeposits[token]` to underflow, then `safeTransfer` attempts to move tokens the contract may not have. Even if the transfer reverts, the unchecked underflow corrupts accounting; if the contract holds enough tokens (from other users' deposits), the attacker drains them.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits 1 unit of token. 2) Attacker calls `emergencyWithdraw(token, hugeAmount)` where hugeAmount > their balance but ≤ contract's token holdings. 3) `unchecked` subtraction underflows `balances[attacker][token]` to a massive number and `totalDeposits[token]` underflows. 4) `safeTransfer` sends `hugeAmount` of tokens to attacker, draining other users' deposits.
hypotheses.impact: Direct theft of all deposited tokens of that type; corrupted `balances` and `totalDeposits` state; protocol insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add an explicit `if (balances[user][token] < amount) revert InsufficientBalance();` check and remove the `unchecked` block (or keep unchecked only after the check).

hypotheses.title: totalDeposits underflow in emergencyWithdraw corrupts liquidity accounting
hypotheses.description: `_processWithdrawal` decrements `totalDeposits[token]` inside `unchecked`. Since `emergencyWithdraw` has no balance check, an attacker can withdraw more than their own balance, causing `totalDeposits[token]` to underflow to a near-2^256 value. This corrupts the reported total liquidity and any logic relying on it, while the contract's real token balance is drained.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits 1 unit of token T. 2) Attacker calls `emergencyWithdraw(T, totalDeposits[T] + 1)` (or any amount exceeding their balance). 3) `totalDeposits[T]` underflows to a huge number. 4) Attacker repeats to drain the contract's real token balance.
hypotheses.impact: `getTotalLiquidity` returns absurd values; any downstream integration relying on `totalDeposits` is misled; combined with the balance underflow, all funds can be drained.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove `unchecked` and enforce a balance check in `_processWithdrawal`; also validate `amount <= totalDeposits[token]`.

hypotheses.title: fillOrder() does not verify quoteToken matches order pair
hypotheses.description: `fillOrder` uses `order.quoteToken` and `order.baseToken` from storage, so the pair is fixed, but it never checks that the taker's balances are being debited/credited consistently with the order's declared pair — this is fine — however the maker's quote credit is added to `balances[order.maker][order.quoteToken]` without ensuring the maker actually wants that token. More critically, the function does not validate that `order.baseToken != order.quoteToken`, allowing a maker to create a self-referential pair where the same token is both base and quote, and a taker's fill can be used to manipulate balances.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker places an order with `baseToken == quoteToken == T`. 2. Attacker (or colluding taker) calls `fillOrder` with amount A. 3. Taker's T balance is debited `A*P/1e18` and credited `A`; maker's T balance is credited `A*P/1e18`. 4. Depending on P, one side gains free T at the other's expense, and the linked-list bookkeeping for the pair is corrupted.
hypotheses.impact: Balance manipulation and potential theft when P ≠ 1e18; corrupted order book for the token pair.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `if (baseToken == quoteToken) revert InvalidPrice();` in `placeOrder`.

hypotheses.title: fillOrder ignores maker's price sanity and allows arbitrary price orders
hypotheses.description: `placeOrder` accepts any nonzero `price` with no check against `MAX_PRICE_DEVIATION` (which is declared but never used) and no oracle reference. A maker can post an order at an absurd price (e.g., 1e30 or 1 wei) and a taker who trusts the orderbook or an automated router will fill it, draining the taker's quote balance at a manipulated rate. The constant `MAX_PRICE_DEVIATION` is dead code, so the intended 1% parity guard is never enforced.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker places a tiny order (>= MIN_ORDER_SIZE) with `price = 1` (or `price = 1e30`) for a stablecoin pair. 2) A taker/router that reads `getOrders` and fills without independent price validation executes `fillOrder`. 3) Taker's quote tokens are swapped at the attacker's chosen rate; attacker captures the spread.
hypotheses.impact: Takers (including automated MPP payment routers) can be drained at arbitrary exchange rates; loss of funds for any counterparty relying on the orderbook price.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce `MAX_PRICE_DEVIATION` against a trusted reference (oracle or 1:1 parity) in `placeOrder`, and reject orders outside the band.

hypotheses.title: withdraw() transfers tokens before decrementing balances (reentrancy)
hypotheses.description: `withdraw()` performs `IERC20(token).safeTransfer(msg.sender, amount)` BEFORE decrementing `balances[msg.sender][token]` and `totalDeposits[token]`. If the token is an ERC-777 style token or otherwise invokes a callback on the recipient (TIP-20 tokens with hooks/policy callbacks), the recipient can reenter `withdraw()` while the balance is still unchanged, draining the contract's token reserves far beyond their recorded balance.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits a small amount of a callback-capable token. 2) Attacker calls `withdraw(token, amount)`. 3) During `safeTransfer`, the token invokes a hook on the attacker's contract. 4) The hook reenters `withdraw()` (or `emergencyWithdraw()`) repeatedly, each time passing the balance check because the decrement hasn't happened yet. 5) Each reentrant call transfers tokens out; the final decrement only subtracts the original amount once.
hypotheses.impact: Full drain of the DEX's token reserves; `totalDeposits` accounting becomes inconsistent with actual holdings, insolvency for other users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Apply the checks-effects-interactions pattern: decrement `balances[msg.sender][token]` and `totalDeposits[token]` before calling `safeTransfer`, or add a nonReentrant guard.

hypotheses.title: fillOrder ignores price deviation cap, allowing arbitrary exchange rates
hypotheses.description: `MAX_PRICE_DEVIATION` is declared but never enforced in `placeOrder` or `fillOrder`. A maker can post an order at any price (e.g. 1 base token for 1e30 quote tokens), and a taker who is unaware or a victim of a malicious front-end can be forced to pay an arbitrarily large quote amount. The constant is dead code, so the intended 1% parity guard does not exist.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker places an order with `price` set to an extreme value (e.g. 1e30) for a small `amount`. 2) A taker (or an automated MPP settlement path) fills the order, paying `amount * price / 1e18` quote tokens. 3) Attacker receives vastly more quote tokens than the base tokens are worth.
hypotheses.impact: Takers can be drained of quote tokens at unfair rates; the stablecoin-pair invariant is broken; loss of funds for any user who fills a malicious order.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce `MAX_PRICE_DEVIATION` in `placeOrder` (and/or `fillOrder`) by requiring `price` to be within 1% of 1e18 for stablecoin pairs.

hypotheses.title: No reentrancy guard on deposit/withdraw/fillOrder
hypotheses.description: `withdraw` performs `safeTransfer` before decrementing `balances[msg.sender][token]` and `totalDeposits[token]`. A malicious TIP-20 token (or a token with a transfer hook) can reenter `withdraw` during the `safeTransfer` and drain the contract before the balance is reduced. The same pattern exists in `_processWithdrawal` (used by `emergencyWithdraw`) and in `fillOrder` (state updates after external calls are not present, but `deposit` uses `safeTransferFrom` before crediting, which is safe).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker deploys a malicious ERC20 that calls back into `withdraw` on `transfer`. 2. Attacker deposits the malicious token. 3. Attacker calls `withdraw(token, amount)`. 4. During `safeTransfer`, the token reenters `withdraw` with the same `amount`; the balance check still passes because the decrement hasn't happened yet. 5. Repeat until contract is drained.
hypotheses.impact: Full drain of the malicious token's deposits (and any other token if the reentrant call targets a different token with a shared balance check bypass).
hypotheses.recommendation: Apply the checks-effects-interactions pattern: decrement `balances` and `totalDeposits` before `safeTransfer`, and add a `nonReentrant` modifier.

hypotheses.title: fillOrder rounds quoteAmount down, letting takers pay less than owed
hypotheses.description: `quoteAmount = (amount * price) / 1e18` truncates toward zero. For any `amount * price` not divisible by 1e18, the taker pays strictly less than the exact price, and the maker receives less than entitled. Repeated small fills (each ≥ MIN_ORDER_SIZE but with prices that produce remainders) let a taker systematically underpay, and the maker's locked base tokens are released at a discount. Rounding should favour the protocol/maker, not the taker.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker places many small fills against a maker's order using an `amount` chosen so `amount * price % 1e18` is just under 1e18 (maximizing the truncated fraction). 2) Each fill transfers `floor(amount*price/1e18)` quote tokens to the maker. 3) Over many fills the attacker extracts value equal to the accumulated truncation remainders, while the maker's order is fully consumed at a discount.
hypotheses.impact: Maker loses a fraction of expected quote tokens per fill; cumulative value leakage from makers to takers; mispriced fills relative to the stated price.
hypotheses.recommendation: Round `quoteAmount` up (ceil) so the taker always pays at least the exact price, or require exact divisibility.

hypotheses.title: fillOrder does not verify order price against current market / oracle
hypotheses.description: Orders persist indefinitely with their original `price`; there is no timestamp, expiry, or oracle freshness check. A maker can leave a stale order at an old price and a taker (or router) will fill it at that stale rate even if the market has moved. Combined with the absence of `MAX_PRICE_DEVIATION` enforcement, this allows stale-price exploitation.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker places an order at a price that becomes favorable to them after a market move. 2) Victim's router fills the stale order. 3) Attacker profits at victim's expense.
hypotheses.impact: Takers fill at stale prices; loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add order expiry timestamps and/or validate `order.price` against a fresh oracle before filling.

hypotheses.title: deposit() credits balance after external transferFrom (reentrancy via callback token)
hypotheses.description: `deposit()` calls `IERC20(token).safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount)` before updating `balances[msg.sender][token]` and `totalDeposits[token]`. A callback-capable token (ERC-777/TIP-20 with hooks) can invoke code on the sender during the transfer, allowing reentrancy into `deposit()`, `withdraw()`, `placeOrder()`, or `fillOrder()` while the balance state is stale, enabling double-counting or draining.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker uses a token that calls a hook on `from` during `transferFrom`. 2) Attacker calls `deposit(token, amount)`. 3) During `safeTransferFrom`, the hook reenters `withdraw()` or `placeOrder()` using the pre-deposit balance state, or reenters `deposit()` to double-credit. 4) State ends up inconsistent, allowing withdrawal of more than deposited.
hypotheses.impact: Balance inflation and potential drain of other users' funds; incorrect `totalDeposits` accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Update `balances` and `totalDeposits` before the external `safeTransferFrom`, or add a reentrancy guard.

hypotheses.title: fillOrder lets taker fill own order to mint balances / self-deal
hypotheses.description: `fillOrder` does not prevent `msg.sender` from being the order's maker. A maker can fill their own order, moving quote tokens from their own balance to their own balance and base tokens back to themselves, while `order.remaining` decreases. This allows a maker to "consume" their own order without external counterparty, and combined with the linked-list removal logic can be used to manipulate orderbook state or wash-trade balances.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker places an order selling base for quote. 2. Attacker calls `fillOrder(orderId, amount)` on their own order. 3. Balances are debited/credited to the same account (net zero for quote, base returned), but `remaining` decreases and the order may be removed. 4. Attacker uses this to erase orders or manipulate book state without real trades.
hypotheses.impact: Orderbook state manipulation; wash trading; potential to bypass intended maker/taker separation and distort liquidity accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `if (msg.sender == order.maker) revert Unauthorized();` in `fillOrder`.

hypotheses.title: getOrders unbounded loop can be gas-DoS'd by attacker placing many orders
hypotheses.description: `getOrders` iterates the linked list up to `maxOrders`, but the caller controls `maxOrders` and the list length is attacker-controlled. An attacker can place a very large number of minimum-size orders for a token pair, making the linked list extremely long. Any off-chain consumer (LCA routing, UI) calling `getOrders` with a large `maxOrders` will hit the block gas limit and revert, effectively freezing the order book view. Since `placeOrder` has no cap on orders per pair, the list can grow unbounded.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker repeatedly calls `placeOrder(base, quote, price, MIN_ORDER_SIZE)` with distinct order IDs. 2. Linked list for `(base, quote)` grows to thousands of nodes. 3. Any call to `getOrders(base, quote, largeMax)` reverts out-of-gas. 4. Routing/UI cannot read the book; takers cannot discover orders.
hypotheses.impact: Order book becomes unreadable; DEX effectively frozen for that pair; integrators (MPP routing) break.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap orders per pair, or paginate `getOrders` with a bounded `maxOrders` and a `startId` cursor; consider a max list length enforced in `placeOrder`.

hypotheses.title: _cancelOrder deletes only partial order fields, leaving remaining/prev/next stale
hypotheses.description: `_cancelOrder` deletes `maker`, `baseToken`, `quoteToken`, `price`, and `amount`, but does not delete `remaining`, `prev`, or `next`. Since `order.maker == address(0)` is the existence check, the order is treated as non-existent, but stale `prev`/`next` values remain. If a new order reuses the same ID (impossible with the counter) or if any code path reads these fields without checking maker, stale data could be used. More concretely, `getOrder` returns the full struct including stale `remaining`, misleading integrators.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker cancels an order. 2) External integrator calls `getOrder(orderId)` and reads `remaining` (non-zero) and `prev`/`next`, incorrectly assuming the order is still live. 3) Integrator routes a fill against a non-existent order, reverting or misrouting.
hypotheses.impact: Misleading view data; potential integration failures; no direct fund loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Delete the entire struct with `delete orders[orderId];` in `_cancelOrder`.

hypotheses.title: placeOrder does not verify baseToken != quoteToken, enabling self-dealing wash trades
hypotheses.description: `placeOrder` allows `baseToken == quoteToken`. A maker can place an order selling token T for token T at an arbitrary price. A taker (or the maker themselves via a second account) can fill it, moving balances between accounts without economic substance. This can be used to wash-trade, inflate volume, or manipulate any off-chain reward/epoch accounting that keys off `OrderFilled` events.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker places an order with `baseToken == quoteToken == T` and a chosen price. 2) Attacker fills it from another account. 3) `OrderFilled` events are emitted, and balances shift between the attacker's accounts. 4) Any reward epoch or volume-based incentive that reads these events is gamed.
hypotheses.impact: Wash trading; manipulation of any volume-based rewards; misleading on-chain activity; potential reward farming if incentives are added.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert in `placeOrder` if `baseToken == quoteToken`.

hypotheses.title: fillOrder rounding allows zero-quote fills draining maker's base for free
hypotheses.description: `quoteAmount = (amount * price) / 1e18` truncates. If `price < 1e18` and `amount` is small, `quoteAmount` can round to 0, but the code reverts on `quoteAmount == 0`. However, for `price` slightly above 0 and `amount` chosen so `quoteAmount` is 1 wei, the taker pays 1 wei of quote and receives `amount` base tokens. With `MIN_ORDER_SIZE = 1e6` and price granularity, a taker can repeatedly fill tiny amounts paying near-zero quote, extracting base tokens from the maker at a fraction of fair value. The maker's order is drained cheaply.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Maker places order with price = 1 (1 wei quote per 1e18 base). 2. Attacker calls `fillOrder(orderId, 1e6)` → quoteAmount = 1e6 * 1 / 1e18 = 0 → reverts. 3. Attacker instead uses amount = 1e18 → quoteAmount = 1 wei, receives 1e18 base for 1 wei quote. 4. Repeat until order drained.
hypotheses.impact: Maker's base tokens are sold for essentially nothing; value extraction from makers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce a minimum `quoteAmount` (e.g., `>= MIN_ORDER_SIZE`) or round up (`(amount * price + 1e18 - 1) / 1e18`).

hypotheses.title: Fee-on-transfer / rebasing tokens break deposit accounting
hypotheses.description: `deposit` credits `balances[msg.sender][token] += amount` and `totalDeposits[token] += amount` based solely on the requested `amount`, without measuring the actual received balance delta. If the token charges a transfer fee or rebases, the contract receives less than `amount`, so recorded balances exceed real holdings. Withdrawals then fail or drain other users' deposits.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits a fee-on-transfer token T with amount A; contract receives A - fee. 2) Attacker's recorded balance is A, but contract holds A - fee. 3) Attacker withdraws A (or trades against other users' balances), extracting the fee shortfall from other depositors' funds. 4) Contract becomes undercollateralized.
hypotheses.impact: Insolvency of the DEX; honest users cannot withdraw their full balances; attacker profits at the expense of the pool.
hypotheses.recommendation: Measure the actual received amount via balance delta (`before`/`after`) and credit only that, or explicitly restrict supported tokens to non-fee, non-rebasing assets.

hypotheses.title: Price decimals mismatch between 18-decimal price and 6-decimal tokens
hypotheses.description: `price` is documented as 18 decimals and `quoteAmount = amount * price / 1e18`. But `MIN_ORDER_SIZE = 1e6` and the tokens are TIP-20 stablecoins with 6 decimals. If `amount` is in 6-decimal base units and `price` is 18-decimal, the resulting `quoteAmount` is in 6-decimal units only when `price` is scaled to 1e18 per 1e6 base units — i.e., the code implicitly assumes `price` is "quote per base" in 18-decimal fixed point but the base amount is 6-decimal, so a 1:1 price must be `1e12`, not `1e18`. A maker posting `price = 1e18` (naive 1:1) will charge takers 1e12x the intended amount.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker posts an order with `price = 1e18` (looks like 1:1 to a naive integrator). 2) Taker fills a small `amount`; `quoteAmount = amount * 1e18 / 1e18 = amount`, but since base is 6-dec and quote is 6-dec, the taker pays 1 base unit of quote per 1 base unit of base — actually correct only if both are 6-dec. However any integrator computing price off-chain in 18-dec will mis-scale. More critically, a maker can post `price = 1e12` intending 1:1 and takers using 18-dec math will overpay by 1e6x.
hypotheses.impact: Systematic mispricing; takers overpay or makers underpay depending on which convention is used; accounting drift.
hypotheses.recommendation: Normalize both token decimals explicitly (fetch `decimals()` and scale) or document and enforce a single canonical price scale with a helper.

hypotheses.title: cancel() refunds before fully clearing order, enabling reentrancy double-refund
hypotheses.description: `_cancelOrder()` credits `balances[maker][baseToken] += refund` and emits the event, but does not zero `order.remaining` (only deletes maker/baseToken/quoteToken/price/amount). If a callback-capable token or a reentrant path lets the maker call `cancel(orderId)` again before `maker` is fully cleared, or if `fillOrder` is called on the partially-cleared order, the `remaining` value can be refunded twice or the order can be filled after cancellation.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Maker places order. 2) Maker calls `cancel(orderId)`. 3) During any token callback (or via a reentrant call from a hook), maker reenters `cancel(orderId)` — `order.maker` may still be set in the same transaction if the delete hasn't completed, or `fillOrder` reads stale `remaining`. 4) Maker receives refund twice or taker fills a cancelled order.
hypotheses.impact: Double refund of locked tokens; maker drains contract balance; orderbook integrity broken.
hypotheses.recommendation: Zero out `order.remaining` and all fields before crediting the refund, and add a reentrancy guard.

hypotheses.title: No deadline/nonce on orders enabling stale execution and replay
hypotheses.description: Orders carry no deadline or nonce and are executed purely by on-chain order ID. Once placed, an order remains fillable indefinitely at the stored price, and there is no mechanism to invalidate a signed intent off-chain. In a meta-transaction or off-chain-signed order flow (as implied by the MPP/payment-lane design), a signed order could be replayed or executed long after the maker's intended window, at a stale price.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Maker signs/places an order at a favorable price. 2. Market moves; maker intends to cancel but the order persists. 3. Attacker (taker) fills the stale order at the old price, extracting value from the maker. 4. No deadline check prevents execution.
hypotheses.impact: Makers forced to trade at stale prices; value extraction from makers; no time-bounded execution guarantee.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a `deadline` field to orders and revert in `fillOrder` if `block.timestamp > deadline`; include a nonce for any off-chain signed order flow.

hypotheses.title: _removeFilledOrder leaves stale remaining/amount fields readable
hypotheses.description: When an order is fully filled, `_removeFilledOrder` only zeroes `prev`, `next`, and `maker`, leaving `baseToken`, `quoteToken`, `price`, `amount`, and `remaining` intact. Since `order.maker == address(0)` is the existence check, the order is treated as nonexistent, but the stale fields remain readable via `getOrder` and could confuse integrators or off-chain indexers relying on those fields.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker fully fills an order. 2. `_removeFilledOrder` clears only maker/prev/next. 3. Off-chain consumers reading `getOrder` see stale token/price/amount data for a "deleted" order, potentially mis-routing or mis-pricing.
hypotheses.impact: Off-chain/indexer confusion; potential mis-integration; no direct fund loss on-chain.
hypotheses.recommendation: Delete the entire order struct (or all fields) in `_removeFilledOrder` to match `_cancelOrder`'s cleanup.

hypotheses.title: fillOrder does not credit maker's base-token balance on partial fills correctly across price rounding
hypotheses.description: `quoteAmount` is computed as `(amount * price) / 1e18` and truncated. For small `amount` and low `price`, `quoteAmount` can round to 0, which is caught by `if (quoteAmount == 0) revert`. However, for repeated tiny fills the maker receives less quote than the proportional value of the base sold, and the taker pays less. More importantly, `order.remaining` is decremented by `amount` while the maker's quote credit is truncated, so the maker can end up selling base tokens for less than the stated price over many fills.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker places a maker order at a price where `amount * price / 1e18` truncates heavily (e.g. price = 1, amount = 1e6). 2) Attacker (as taker) fills in many small chunks so each fill's `quoteAmount` is truncated down. 3) Maker receives less quote than the nominal price implies; taker pays less.
hypotheses.impact: Systematic value leakage from makers to takers; unfair distribution of proceeds; maker loses funds proportional to rounding error.
hypotheses.recommendation: Round `quoteAmount` up (favor the maker) or accumulate a remainder per order so truncation is not lost.

hypotheses.title: fillOrder credits taker base tokens without checking maker's locked balance consistency
hypotheses.description: When an order is placed, the maker's base tokens are deducted from `balances[maker][baseToken]` and held implicitly by the order's `remaining` field, but `totalDeposits[baseToken]` is never adjusted. On fill, the taker's base balance is credited and the maker's quote balance is credited, but the base tokens "held" by the order are never reconciled against `totalDeposits`. This creates a divergence between `totalDeposits` and actual token custody, and the maker's base tokens are effectively double-counted (removed from balance but still counted in totalDeposits).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Maker places an order, reducing `balances[maker][base]` but leaving `totalDeposits[base]` unchanged. 2) `getTotalLiquidity` reports inflated liquidity. 3) Any logic or integration relying on `totalDeposits` (e.g., solvency checks, external routers) makes incorrect assumptions, and if a future function uses `totalDeposits` for withdrawals, funds can be misallocated.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect accounting of total liquidity; potential for future insolvency if `totalDeposits` is used as a source of truth for payouts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Either track locked amounts separately in `totalDeposits` accounting or document that `totalDeposits` excludes locked order amounts and ensure no logic depends on it for solvency.

hypotheses.title: placeOrder allows baseToken == quoteToken, corrupting linked list and balances
hypotheses.description: `placeOrder` does not reject `baseToken == quoteToken`. When both are the same, the order is inserted into `orderHeads[token][token]`, and on fill the taker's balance for that token is both debited (quote) and credited (base), and the maker's balance is credited with the same token. This creates self-referential swaps that can be used to manipulate the linked list and balances, and combined with the missing cancel authorization, an attacker can grief the orderbook.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker places an order with `baseToken == quoteToken` and a favorable price. 2) Attacker (or another account) fills it, moving tokens between balances in a way that nets to zero for the taker but credits the maker. 3) Attacker uses this to inflate balances or manipulate `totalDeposits` accounting.
hypotheses.impact: Balance/accounting manipulation; potential to inflate balances and drain via `emergencyWithdraw` (combined with the underflow bug).
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `if (baseToken == quoteToken) revert InvalidAmount();` in `placeOrder`.

hypotheses.title: totalDeposits not decremented on fill, drifts from real holdings
hypotheses.description: `fillOrder` moves balances between users but never updates `totalDeposits` for either token. `totalDeposits` is only adjusted in `deposit`/`withdraw`. Since fills don't change the contract's aggregate holdings, this is consistent for the sum, but `getTotalLiquidity` is documented as "total deposited amount" and is used as a liquidity signal; it will not reflect tokens that have been swapped out of one token into another via fills, so the reported liquidity per token diverges from actual token holdings whenever fills occur.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable for theft, but any external integrator (e.g., LCA routing, MPP settlement) relying on `getTotalLiquidity` to size swaps or verify solvency will misprice or over-allocate, potentially causing failed settlements or misrouted liquidity.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong accounting signal; integrators may over-commit liquidity that isn't actually present in a given token, leading to failed withdrawals or misrouted payments.
hypotheses.recommendation: Either document `totalDeposits` as "net user deposits" and stop using it as a liquidity oracle, or update it on every balance-moving operation to reflect real token holdings.

hypotheses.title: placeOrder allows self-crossing and price inversion without validation
hypotheses.description: `placeOrder` does not validate that `baseToken != quoteToken`, nor that the price is consistent with the pair direction. A maker can create an order where base and quote are the same token, or where the price is inverted relative to the intended pair, and `fillOrder` will happily execute it, moving balances between the same token or at an inverted rate.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker places an order with `baseToken == quoteToken` and `price = 1e18`. 2) A taker fills it; balances are debited and credited in the same token, but the maker's locked amount is released and the taker's balance is reduced by `quoteAmount` while credited `amount` — net loss to taker if `quoteAmount > amount` due to rounding or price.
hypotheses.impact: Confusing accounting, potential taker loss, orderbook pollution.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert if `baseToken == quoteToken` and validate price direction against a canonical pair ordering.

hypotheses.title: fillOrder() allows maker to reenter via callback token and manipulate order state
hypotheses.description: `fillOrder()` mutates `balances` and `order.remaining` but the maker's quote-token credit and the taker's base-token credit are pure internal accounting (no external call), so direct reentrancy is limited. However, if the maker is a contract and the base/quote tokens are callback-capable, the maker can reenter `cancel()` or `fillOrder()` on the same order during any token interaction triggered elsewhere, and `_removeFilledOrder` only clears `maker`/`prev`/`next` while leaving `remaining` and other fields, allowing stale-order reuse in edge cases.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Maker places an order. 2) Taker fills it partially; before `_removeFilledOrder` runs on full fill, a callback token (if any transfer occurs) lets the maker reenter `cancel()` to refund `remaining` while the order is still linked, or reenter `fillOrder()` to double-fill. 3) Maker extracts refund plus fill proceeds.
hypotheses.impact: Double-spend of locked tokens; maker can extract more than the order's value; linked-list corruption.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a `nonReentrant` guard to `fillOrder`, `cancel`, and `placeOrder`, and fully clear all order fields (including `remaining`) in `_removeFilledOrder`.

hypotheses.title: fillOrder price math truncation lets taker pay zero quote for base
hypotheses.description: `quoteAmount = (amount * price) / 1e18` truncates toward zero. For small `amount` or low `price`, the result can round down, and the code only reverts if `quoteAmount == 0`. A taker can choose `amount` such that `quoteAmount` is 1 wei while receiving a disproportionately large `amount` of base tokens, or exploit rounding to systematically underpay the maker across many fills.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker places many small fills against a maker's order. 2. Each fill's `quoteAmount` truncates down, so attacker pays less than the true proportional price. 3. Attacker accumulates base tokens at a discount; maker receives less quote than owed.
hypotheses.impact: Maker underpaid; value leakage from makers to takers; cumulative loss over many fills.
hypotheses.recommendation: Round `quoteAmount` up (e.g., `(amount * price + 1e18 - 1) / 1e18`) or enforce a minimum quote amount per fill.

hypotheses.title: fillOrder quoteAmount cast to uint128 can silently truncate
hypotheses.description: `quoteAmount` is computed as a uint256 and then cast to uint128 in multiple places (`balances[msg.sender][order.quoteToken] -= uint128(quoteAmount)`, `balances[order.maker][order.quoteToken] += uint128(quoteAmount)`). If `amount * price / 1e18` exceeds `type(uint128).max`, the cast truncates silently, allowing the taker to pay less than the true price while receiving the full base amount. The check `balances[msg.sender][quoteToken] < quoteAmount` uses the uint256 value, but the actual debit uses the truncated uint128.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker places a large order or finds one with a high price. 2) Attacker calls `fillOrder` with an `amount` such that `quoteAmount > 2^128`. 3) The uint128 cast truncates the debit, so the attacker pays far less quote tokens than required while receiving the full base amount. 4) Maker is underpaid; attacker profits.
hypotheses.impact: Taker underpays maker; maker loses funds; accounting mismatch between intended and actual transfer amounts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert if `quoteAmount > type(uint128).max` before casting, or use uint256 for balances.

hypotheses.title: placeOrder() allows maker to place order against own balance without lock isolation
hypotheses.description: `placeOrder` deducts `amount` from `balances[msg.sender][baseToken]` but does not track a separate `locked` balance per order. When `cancel` is called (by anyone, see finding 1), the refund is credited back to `balances[maker][baseToken]`. Because `fillOrder` credits the maker's quote balance but never touches the maker's base balance for the filled portion, and `_removeFilledOrder` does not refund the unfilled remainder, a partially filled order that is later cancelled refunds only `order.remaining` — which is correct — but the maker's original `amount` deduction is never reconciled against `order.amount` if the order is removed via `_removeFilledOrder` while `remaining > 0` (impossible) — however the real issue is that `cancel` can be called on a fully-filled order whose `maker` was zeroed, reverting, but a partially filled order's `remaining` is refunded while the filled portion's base was already credited to takers, so accounting is consistent. The exploitable gap is that `placeOrder` does not prevent a maker from placing multiple orders that collectively exceed their balance because each `placeOrder` re-checks `balances[msg.sender][baseToken]` after deduction, which is correct.
hypotheses.attackPath: No direct exploit path identified beyond the cancel/fill issues already reported.
hypotheses.impact: None beyond the reported findings.
hypotheses.recommendation: No change needed for this specific concern.

hypotheses.title: Zero-amount fills blocked but dust fills still drain maker via rounding
hypotheses.description: `fillOrder` rejects `amount == 0` and `quoteAmount == 0`, but allows `amount = 1` (below MIN_ORDER_SIZE, which is only enforced on `placeOrder`). A taker can fill 1 unit at a time; with a price that yields `quoteAmount == 0` it reverts, but with a price yielding `quoteAmount == 1` the taker pays 1 quote unit for 1 base unit regardless of the true price, and the maker's order is consumed in dust increments. Combined with the truncation in the same function, this lets a taker grind a maker's order at near-zero cost.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker repeatedly calls `fillOrder(orderId, 1)` against a maker's order. 2) Each call consumes 1 base unit and pays `floor(price/1e18)` quote units. 3) If `price < 1e18`, quoteAmount is 0 and reverts; if `price ≥ 1e18` but small, the attacker pays a tiny amount per unit, effectively buying base tokens at a rounded-down price.
hypotheses.impact: Maker's order is consumed at unfavorable rounding; small but repeatable value leakage; griefing of makers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce `amount >= MIN_ORDER_SIZE` in `fillOrder` as well, and round `quoteAmount` up.

hypotheses.title: fillOrder() price/amount rounding lets taker underpay via dust fills
hypotheses.description: `quoteAmount = (amount * price) / 1e18` truncates. A taker can repeatedly fill tiny `amount` values where `quoteAmount` rounds down to a smaller value than the true proportional price, extracting base tokens at a discount. The `quoteAmount == 0` check only blocks exact-zero cases, not systematic dust-fill underpayment.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker places many small `fillOrder` calls with `amount` chosen so `(amount * price) % 1e18` is large relative to `amount`. 2) Each fill pays slightly less quote than the fair price. 3) Over many fills, attacker accumulates base tokens below market price, draining maker's order value.
hypotheses.impact: Maker receives less quote than entitled; value leakage from makers to takers; orderbook pricing becomes exploitable.
hypotheses.recommendation: Round `quoteAmount` up (ceiling division) or enforce a minimum fill size such that rounding error is bounded.
